title: Simple arithmetic systems can produce highly complex behavior

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Simple arithmetic systems can produce highly complex behavior

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: When systems based on numbers are studied by computer experiment rather than by mathematical analysis, even very simple ones turn out to produce highly complex behavior.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: if one ignores the need for analysis and instead just looks at the results of computer experiments, then one quickly finds that even rather simple systems based on numbers can lead to highly complex behavior.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 4, “Systems Based on Numbers”; section “The Notion of Numbers” (from p. 115), pp. 115–116. Scope: simple iterative systems defined by arithmetic operations on numbers

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch04-02: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.81

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The existential claim can be settled by reproducible computations on precisely defined maps, with many public sequences available for cross-checking. Standard analyses can confirm complex finite behavior even though they may not prove all asymptotic properties.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Specify simple arithmetic maps and seeds, compute long trajectories, and quantify periodicity, growth, compressibility, and statistical irregularity. A single robust low-description-length example with high behavioral complexity confirms the existential core.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Highly complex remains dependent on chosen metrics.

Finite runs can hide eventual periodicity.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.9
analysis feasibility: 0.9
data adequacy: 0.7
discriminating power: 0.82
operationalizability: 0.72

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim is existential and the examples are elementary iterations. Public arbitrary-precision arithmetic recomputes them far past the pictures in the book, and a detected closed form or eventual period would refute a specific example while a persistent irregular pattern confirms the 'can.' That is enough to settle the claim as stated, with the usual limit that statistical tests do not prove infinite randomness.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compute long orbits of simple arithmetic iterations, including successive powers of 3 in base 2, and test the digit arrays and size series for periodicity, nesting, and statistical irregularity. A long irregular orbit confirms that simple number systems can be complex; every simple arithmetic system in a declared class collapsing to a short closed form would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A finite irregular prefix can still have a regularity that appears only at larger scales.

'Highly complex' has to be read as failing standard periodicity and compression tests rather than as a proved absence of a formula.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.7
data existence: 0.9
analysis feasibility: 0.95
data adequacy: 0.85
discriminating power: 0.65

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Within the family of the simplest arithmetic iterations, repeated multiplication by a fixed small integer m viewed as a base-b digit array (Wolfram's opening example, pp. 116-120), some members produce digit arrays whose interior is incompressible with digit frequencies indistinguishable from uniform, while the trivial members (m a power of b) are detected as highly compressible.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py iterates x -> m x from 1 for 3000 steps for each of the 64 (m, b) pairs using Python integers, converts each power to base-b digits, keeps the interior 25%-75% of digit positions per row, concatenates (one byte per digit) and lzma-compresses; it also computes digit-value frequencies in the window. Per-pair results are in derived/pairs.csv. Runtime about 4 minutes.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Family: all pairs (m, b) with multiplier m in 2..9 and base b in 2..9, iterating x_{t+1} = m x_t from x_0 = 1 for t = 1..T = 3000 (i.e. the digits of m^t). For each pair build the digit array of rows m^t written in base b; take the interior window of each row consisting of digit positions between 25% and 75% of that row's length (least significant digit = position 0), concatenate all interior digits in row order into one byte string (one digit per byte). Measure (i) bits per digit = 8 * lzma(preset 9|EXTREME) compressed size / number of digits; (ii) maximum absolute deviation of any digit-value frequency from 1/b. A pair is 'complex' if (i) >= 0.8 * log2(b) and (ii) <= 0.02; a pair is 'simple' if (i) < 0.1 * log2(b). The claim PASSES if at least one pair with m not a power of b is 'complex' AND every pair with m a power of b (m = b^j, j >= 1, e.g. (2,2), (4,2), (8,2), (9,3), (3,3), ...) is 'simple' (validity check that the measure separates trivially regular digit arrays). Reported, not decisive: how many of the 64 pairs are complex, and whether the pairs with m and b sharing all prime factors (e.g. (6,2), (4,8), (2,4)) behave differently.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if no pair with m not a power of b is 'complex' (every such digit array compresses below 0.8 log2(b) bits per digit or has digit frequencies deviating from uniform by more than 0.02). If any trivial pair (m a power of b) is not 'simple', the measure lacks discriminating power and the verdict is inconclusive (not-operationalizable).

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: pairs (m,b) with m not a power of b whose interior digit array is 'complex' by the pre-registered criteria

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Wolfram's 'even rather simple systems based on numbers can lead to highly complex behavior' (p. 115) is illustrated by the digit sequences of successive powers (p. 116-120: 2^t in base 2 is trivial, 3^t in base 2 looks random). 'Highly complex behavior' is read as digit arrays that a general-purpose compressor cannot reduce below 80% of their entropy bound and whose digit frequencies are uniform to within 2%, in explicit contrast to the trivial members of the same family that compress to below 10%. The claim is existential; the family is the smallest natural one containing the book's opening examples. The window excludes the leading digits (biased by Benford-type effects) and trailing digits (eventually periodic in t at fixed position, and all zero when b divides m).

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: Digit arrays of m^t in base b for m, b in 2..9, t = 1..3000 (generated by analysis.py)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The 10 non-complex non-trivial pairs split into two explicable groups: (2,4), (2,8), (4,8), (8,4), (3,9) where m and b are powers of a common integer (the pre-registered 'm is a power of b' control missed this symmetric case; they compress to < 0.001 of the bound, i.e. are trivially regular), and the five m = 6 pairs in bases 2, 3, 4, 8, 9 where the trailing zeros of 6^t = 2^t 3^t occupy 1/log_b(6) of each row and intrude into the fixed 25%-75% window, lowering compression ratios to 0.30-0.83 and biasing digit frequencies.

Incompressibility by lzma over about 3.6 million interior digits (for 3^t in base 2: 1.086 bits/digit, digit frequencies within 0.0004 of 1/2) is evidence against periodic or nested structure at these scales, not a proof of normality; the digits of 3^t in base 2 are not proven to be normal.

The test covers the book's opening family (powers in positional notation) only; the claim's other illustrations in Chapter 4 (e.g. the 3n/2 system, iterated maps) were not tested.
